messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Security Guard
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 49

He walks the perimeter of the office complex three times before his shift starts. Each circuit takes fourteen minutes. He times it. At seventy-one, Robert moves more slowly than he used to, but his eyes never stop scanning—the delivery trucks, the visitors signing in at the glass kiosk, the empty corners of the parking garage. He knows every shadow that doesn't belong. He has to.

It started on April 19, 1995. Robert was working the security desk at the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City. He was forty-three, a former Army MP, proud of his post. That morning he was checking IDs, joking with a secretary about her new haircut. Then the floor lifted. The blast threw him against the wall, filled his ears with a pressure so immense he thought his skull would crack. He remembers the dust, the screams, the broken glass crunching under his boots as he crawled toward the day-care center. He remembers the child he pulled from the rubble—a little boy, maybe three, silent and gray. Robert carried him outside and handed him to a paramedic. The boy's eyes were open but perfectly still. Robert never learned if that boy lived.

For months after, Robert couldn't speak about it. He quit security work altogether. He took a job at a lumberyard, then a hardware store. Nothing fit. His wife, Diane, said he became a different man—short-tempered, sleepless, always checking the locks. He would stop in the middle of a conversation, cock his head, listening for something only he could hear. Fireworks, even a car backfiring, would drop him to the floor. He started drinking in the evenings, not enough to get drunk, just enough to blur the edges of his dreams. But the dreams never blurred. The boy's face, the dust, the angle of broken beams—they replayed behind his eyelids like a broken film.

Twenty years passed. The drinking slowed. The nightmares softened into a kind of low static. Diane convinced him to apply for a security guard job at a corporate campus on the edge of town. He needed purpose, she said. He needed to feel useful again. Robert agreed, but the first week back on a security post, he vomited in the break room. Every person who walked toward the entrance could be carrying something. Every unattended bag was a bomb. He forced himself to stay, to keep his face calm, because panic is a luxury he cannot afford.

Now, at seventy-one, Robert is a fixture. His uniform is pressed, his badge polished. He knows the names of the janitors and the mail clerks. He carries a heavy key ring, and he rattles it as he walks to remind himself that he is awake, that he is here, that this quiet lobby is not the broken building he still sees in his mind. But the vigilance does not rest. When he hears a loud noise—a dropped metal tray in the cafeteria, a door slamming—his heart accelerates before his mind can catch up. He feels the old pressure in his ears. He blinks hard and counts to five. By the fifth count, the world usually settles back to normal.

Diane worries. She tells him he seems alone even when they are together. He watches the news with one eye on the television and one on the street. He can't sit with his back to a restaurant door. He has not been to a sporting event or a concert in twenty-eight years. The only time Robert feels fully present is when he is walking his perimeter, because then his fear has a job to do. It becomes a tool: check the door, scan the vehicle, note the time. The boy is not in the rubble. The dust is not falling. He is an old man with a key ring, doing his rounds. But the film never stops. He only knows how to live inside it.
